## Start-up

Before any pressure is admitted to the protected equipment, it is essential that the readiness of the relief valve is thoroughly proved. The starting point is the nameplate, where the set pressure and the valve size should be read and carefully checked against the equipment data sheet. It should be appreciated that a valve fitted with the wrong set pressure will protect at the wrong limit, whilst a valve of the wrong size may be unable to pass the required relief load. The inlet line should be walked from the equipment nozzle to the valve, and the discharge line should likewise be walked from the valve to its destination, with attention being paid to damage, corrosion, debris that may have been left behind by maintenance activities, and liquid standing in low points of the discharge line. The inlet block valve and the outlet block valve should be proved fully open, and each valve should be secured in the open position by means of its seal or lock, so that the state cannot be changed without being noticed. Every drain on the discharge side should be proved closed and the bonnet drain proved clear. The protected equipment should then be pressurised slowly and in stages, with a hold at each stage of sufficient duration to allow the inlet and discharge flanges to be inspected for leakage. As the pressure approaches the normal operating level, the operator should stand at the valve and listen attentively: below its set pressure, the valve should remain shut, silent, and cold at the outlet. A valve that simmers, chatters, or weeps at normal pressure cannot be regarded as being in service, and in such a case the start-up should be stopped, the equipment depressurised, and the valve reported for removal and bench testing. The start-up record should state the set pressure that was read at the nameplate, the state of the block valves, and the behaviour exhibited by the valve during the first pressurisation.

## Normal operation

For the entire period during which the protected equipment is pressurised, the relief valve should be regarded as being in service, irrespective of whether it is actually called upon to operate. The valve should therefore be included in every round that is carried out. The inlet and outlet block valves should be proved to be still fully open and still secured, and it is important to note that an unsecured valve that is found part-closed must be reported within the same shift, with the equipment being treated as unprotected until such time as the state has been restored and witnessed. The operator should listen at the valve body for any evidence of passing and should compare the temperature of the discharge line with its normal state, since a warm discharge line on a valve that has not lifted indicates that the seat is passing. Following any lift, the valve should be attended until it has reseated, after which the discharge outlet should be checked for frost, condensate, or debris that may have been carried up from the line, and the outlet cleared as necessary. Access to the valve and to its block valves should be kept unobstructed at all times, and it should be remembered that the ladders, platforms, and lighting serving the valve form part of its availability. The spindle must never be gagged, the outlet must never be plugged, and a block valve must never be closed in order to silence a passing valve; furthermore, no attempt should be made to adjust the set pressure at the line. Every lift, leak, and passing seat should be entered in the shift log together with the equipment pressure and the time, and the entry should be handed over at the shift change. In normal operation, therefore, the relief valve is proved by the round itself: isolation open, seat tight, and outlet clear.

## Alarms

Two alarms fall within the scope of this chapter. An alarm that is raised elsewhere on the protected equipment should be answered under its own chapter, and the relief valve should be left as found unless the actions that are described below direct otherwise.

High pressure in the protected equipment. The relief valve should be attended without delay. It should be proved that the valve is discharging, by means of the sound at the outlet and the warming of the discharge line, and the equipment pressure should be read. If the pressure is falling, the equipment should be kept steady and the valve watched until it reseats, after which the lift should be reported. If, however, the pressure is held at the alarm level or continues to rise whilst the valve is discharging, the source of pressure should be removed: the feed to the equipment should be stopped and the heating input shut off. The shift supervisor should be informed immediately, and the operator should remain with the equipment until the pressure is falling under control. A discharging valve should never be left unattended, and no block valve should be closed in an attempt to stop the discharge.

Relief valve passing. This alarm is characterised by a warm discharge line, or by audible flow at the valve, with the equipment pressure having returned to its normal level following a lift, or with no lift having been recorded. The shift supervisor should be informed and the equipment pressure placed under close observation. A maintenance request should be raised for the valve to be removed and bench tested, and the passing should be recorded in the shift log. It is essential that the valve is not isolated whilst the equipment remains pressurised, since a passing valve continues to provide protection, whereas isolation would remove the protection entirely. The changeover to a spare valve, where one is provided by the installation, is a planned operation that is governed by its own procedure and does not constitute an alarm response. The alarm actions can therefore be divided according to the pressure: at high pressure, the valve is proved and the source is removed; at normal pressure, the valve is reported and the equipment is protected by observation until such time as the valve can be changed.

## Shutdown

The relief valve should be removed from service only when the protected equipment has been depressurised. The equipment should be let down by its normal route and the pressure brought to zero. Zero should be proved at the gauge, following which the equipment vent should be opened and the state proved again at the vent, since a gauge on its own cannot be relied upon to prove a dead system. The inlet and outlet block valves should be closed, and the isolation locked and tagged. The discharge-line drain should be opened and the line drained fully, with the drain being left open for the whole of the outage. The valve body should be vented through its drain connection before any flange is broken. The valve should be handed over to maintenance only against a recorded isolation, with the record stating the equipment, the valve, the state of the block valves, and the proof of zero pressure that was obtained. Removal, overhaul, set-pressure adjustment, and bench testing are maintenance activities that are governed by the maintenance procedure and should never be attempted at the line. When the tested valve is returned, it should be refitted and restored in accordance with the start-up section of this chapter: the nameplate should be checked against the test certificate, the block valves proved open and secured, and the first pressurisation watched at the valve. A valve that has been out of service can only re-enter service by passing through those checks, and the shutdown record is closed when the return has been entered in the log.

## Alarms

Two alarms belong to this chapter. An alarm raised elsewhere on the protected equipment is answered under its own chapter; the relief valve is left as found unless the actions below direct otherwise.

High pressure in the protected equipment. Attend the relief valve at once. Prove the valve is discharging by the sound at the outlet and the warming of the discharge line, and read the equipment pressure. If the pressure is falling, keep the equipment steady, watch the valve until it reseats, and report the lift. The alarm actions divide by pressure: at high pressure, prove the valve and remove the source; at normal pressure, report the valve and protect the equipment by watch until the valve is changed.

## Shutdown

Remove the relief valve from service only with the protected equipment depressurised. Let the equipment down by its normal route and bring the pressure to zero. Prove zero at the gauge, then open the equipment vent and prove again at the vent; a gauge alone does not prove a dead system. Close the inlet and outlet block valves, and lock and tag the isolation. Open the discharge-line drain and drain the line fully; leave the drain open for the whole outage. Vent the valve body through its drain connection before any flange is broken. Keep the isolation in place until maintenance accepts the handover, and enter the state of the valve and of its lines in the shutdown record. Hand the valve to maintenance only against a recorded isolation: the record states the equipment, the valve, the state of the block valves, and the proof of zero pressure. Removal, overhaul, set-pressure adjustment, and bench testing are maintenance work under the maintenance procedure and are never attempted at the line. When the tested valve returns, refit it and restore it by the start-up section of this chapter: nameplate against test certificate, block valves proved open and secured, first pressurisation watched at the valve. A valve that has been out of service re-enters service only through those checks, and the shutdown record closes when the return is entered in the log.
